content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The BOOK ENTRY defines the fool as one who hears God's word and will not do it — the lawless rather than the unintelligent — with 'Wise' as its opposite. Matthew 7:26 states this identification almost verbatim: 'every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man,' with 7:24 supplying the wise doer as the explicit opposite. Psalm 14:1 confirms the moral rather than intellectual register: the fool's heart-denial of God is immediately cashed out in conduct ('they are corrupt, they have done abominable works'), not in cognitive deficiency. The 'lawless' gloss is carried by the Matthew 7 context itself, where the parallel verdict falls on 'ye that work iniquity' (anomia, 7:23), and by the Psalm's 'abominable works.' The strongest counter-reading — the mainstream view that the fool symbolizes moral-spiritual rebellion or practical godlessness generally — shares the same core referent: a morally disobedient person, not a dull one. It is broader, not contradictory; the entry's 'hears and will not do' is a specification of practical godlessness drawn directly from the cited text, and the counter identifies no supplied text the entry's core cannot explain. Since the counter agrees on the core referent and defeats no assertion actually printed in the entry, the verdict is PERSUADED with FULL support.","book_core_identification":"The biblical fool is the person who hears God's word and refuses to do it — a category of disobedience/lawlessness, not of low intelligence.","book_secondary_elaborations":["The fool is characterized as 'the lawless' (a moral-legal category) rather than 'the unintelligent' (a cognitive category).","The stated opposite of the fool is the Wise (the hearer who does)."],"unsupported_glossary_assertions":[],"chapter_only_objections":["The identification of the ten virgins with the ten tribes / 'virgin of Israel' (1 Kings 11:31; Jeremiah 31) is a typological claim not asserted in the glossary entry and rests partly on the disputed Shem Tov Hebrew Matthew reading 'bridegroom and bride.'","The claim that the oil in Matthew 25 is stored obedience/Spirit-taught truth rather than the Holy Spirit is a chapter-level argument (contra the majority reading) not printed in the entry.","The lamp = commandment and light = law-lived equations (Proverbs 6:23) are chapter derivations beyond the entry's scope.","Reliance on the Hebrew Matthew's 'lazy fools' wording and on nid'akhu/Proverbs 13:9 verbal linkage is text-critical material outside the printed entry.","The Gethsemane 'oil press' typology (Christ's obedience as pressed oil) is homiletic elaboration not asserted by the entry."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The mainstream reading (Responses A–D): the biblical fool symbolizes moral and spiritual rebellion against God — practical godlessness or practical atheism — living as if God does not exist or will not judge, despising wisdom and instruction; the category is ethical-religious, not intellectual, and is broader than 'a hearer who fails to do,' since it can include the arrogant scoffer, the self-trusting rich man, and gradations of Hebrew terms (pethi, kesil, ewil, nabal, letz).","counter_core_identification":"The fool is the practically godless, morally rebellious person who rejects God's authority and wisdom — a moral-religious category rather than an intellectual one.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"SAME_CORE_BROADER","material_core_denial":"No material denial exists. The counter's practically godless rebel and the entry's non-doing hearer can be true of the same referent: Psalm 14:1's fool denies God in the heart and acts corruptly, which is precisely living contrary to the word one possesses; Matthew 7:26 makes 'hearing without doing' the express definition. The counter is a broader label for the same person, and a broader label does not constitute a rival core identification.","counter_case":["Psalm 14:1 defines the fool by heart-denial of God and corruption, without mentioning hearing the word, so 'hears and will not do' could be seen as narrower than the Psalm's picture.","Wisdom literature distinguishes gradations (simple, fool, scoffer; Proverbs 1:22), suggesting 'fool' is not a single fixed definition.","The Pauline 'fool for Christ' inversion (1 Cor 1:18–25; 4:10) shows the word can carry a positive ironic sense the entry does not mention.","Some fools (e.g., the rich fool of Luke 12) are marked by misplaced trust rather than by an explicit scene of hearing and refusing."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Matthew 7:24–27 supplies an explicit, dominical definition: the fool is precisely the one who hears and does not do, and the wise man is his stated opposite — exactly the entry's two printed assertions.","The 'lawless, not unintelligent' gloss is anchored in the immediate context (Matt 7:23, 'ye that work iniquity') and in Psalm 14:1's 'abominable works,' unifying the two cited texts under one moral-legal category.","The entry explains why Scripture pairs fool/wise as doer/non-doer across corpora (Ps 111:10; Deut 4:6; Prov 1:7; 12:15), giving a single operative criterion rather than a diffuse thematic label.","It cleanly explains the parallel verdicts 'I never knew you' (Matt 7:23) and 'I know you not' (Matt 25:12) as falling on the same class: hearers who did not do."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Covers Old Testament fools where no explicit act of hearing is narrated (e.g., Nabal, the rich fool's inner monologue).","Accommodates the lexical spectrum of Hebrew fool-terms and the Pauline ironic usage, which the terse entry does not address."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Matthew 7:24–27 (KJV excerpt of 7:26 printed with the entry) — the explicit hear-but-not-do definition and the wise/foolish opposition","Psalm 14:1 — folly as heart-godlessness expressed in corrupt works, not cognitive deficiency","Matthew 7:23 context ('work iniquity') via the chapter's linkage, grounding 'the lawless'","Proverbs 1:7; 12:15; Psalm 111:10; Deuteronomy 4:6 as corroborating the obedience/wisdom pairing"],"unresolved_objections":["The entry's formula foregrounds the Matthew 7 criterion; Old Testament fool passages describe godless conduct without an explicit hearing scene, so the entry is a synthesis rather than a universal lexical definition — a non-decisive scope observation, since Israel's fools possessed the law they disobeyed.","The entry does not address the Pauline ironic 'fool for Christ' usage, but a glossary of the symbol's negative sense is not obligated to catalogue the ironic inversion."],"confidence":"high"}
